title: `auth` seems to be horribly broken

milestone.title: v4.3
milestone.description: The last version to support python2

body:
## Checklist

- [x] I have included the output of ``celery -A proj report`` in the issue.
      (if you are not able to do this, then at least specify the Celery
       version affected).
- [ ] I have verified that the issue exists against the `master` branch of Celery.

## Report

```
software -> celery:4.2.1 (windowlicker) kombu:4.2.1 py:3.6.6
            billiard:3.5.0.4 redis:2.10.6
platform -> system:Linux arch:64bit imp:CPython
loader   -> celery.loaders.app.AppLoader
settings -> transport:redis results:redis://redis:6379/

[... Django-related settings redacted ...]

CELERY_ACCEPT_CONTENT: ['auth']
CELERY_BROKER_URL: 'redis://redis:6379//'
CELERY_RESULT_BACKEND: 'redis://redis:6379/'
CELERY_RESULT_SERIALIZER: 'auth'
CELERY_SECURITY_CERTIFICATE: '/private/keys/celery/public.pem'
CELERY_SECURITY_CERT_STORE: '/private/keys/celery/*.pem'
CELERY_SECURITY_KEY: '********'
CELERY_TASK_SERIALIZER: 'auth'
```

## Steps to reproduce

### Security setup silently fails because of default settings

I want to be able to check whether incoming tasks are legitimate. Celery seems to offer message signing, which is perfect for this. I've first followed the docs and added this to the Celery setup script:

```
app.conf.update(
    security_key='/private/keys/celery/private.key',
    security_certificate='/private/keys/celery/public.pem',
    security_cert_store='/private/keys/celery/*.pem')

app.setup_security()
```

That wasn't sufficient enough, though. When using an invalid key, Celery wouldn't even report on that. I dug into the source and found an interesting bit in `celery/security/__init__.py` that checks whether the `task_serializer` setting equals `auth`. If it does not, the security setup is silently ignored. This  doesn't seem like a good thing to me, especially as this rather special behaviour doesn't seem to be noted in the docs.

After adding the configuration for `task_serializer='auth'`, certificates do get loaded and security seems to be set up. Celery also reports on invalid keys when this setting is correctly set.

### Enforcing signed messages

Now that signing of messages seemed to be set up, I encountered another error. I can still publish unsigned messages and the workers will happily pick them up. This just totally defeats the purpose of message signing. Why does the worker still process unsigned messages after explicitly setting up message signing?

I now proceeded to setting `accept_content=['auth']` in order to force Celery to only accept `auth`-serialized messages from the broker. After setting this up, unsigned messages finally get "dismissed", as the docs describe it.

### Unsigned messages crash workers

After sending an unsigned message (json serializer, for example) into the queue, the worker still picks them up. It will then check for the content type and notice that it doesn't match `auth`, which I had set up as the only accepted content type (again, otherwise it would totally defeat the purpose of setting up message signing). It will then raise a ContentDisallowed exception in `celery/worker/strategy.py`. This exception is never catched and will therefor *crash the entire worker*.

The worker will actually put the unsigned message *back into the queue after it's crashed on it*. Any other workers that pick the message up, will also crash and put the message back into the queue. This is a potential DOS flaw and this should never happen. Messages should be "dismissed", such as the docs state, but it should *not* crash the entire worker - and potentially all other workers.

### Messages with invalid signature crash workers

The same issue seems to occur for messages that have been signed by a certificate that is not currently in the worker's cert store. A `SecurityError` exception is raised in `celery/security/certificate.py` which is not properly handled. This is another potential DOS flaw, especially as this bug will also restore the unacknowledged message.

### New workers introduce themselves with an unsigned message

I plan on having multiple servers running Celery workers. This set up exposed another bug that may enable DOS attacks. New workers introduce themselves, but don't sign their "introduction message", so to say. I haven't looked into this procedure yet because of lack of time, but it's simple to reproduce:

* Configure workers to have `accept_content = ['auth']` let them use the `auth` serializer
* Spawn the first worker and leave it up
* Spawn a second worker
* Watch the first ánd second worker crash

The exception is as follows:

```
[2018-09-10 02:33:07,446: CRITICAL/MainProcess] Unrecoverable error: ContentDisallowed('Refusing to deserialize disabled content of type json (application/json)',)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/usr/lib/python3.6/site-packages/celery/worker/worker.py", line 205, in start
    self.blueprint.start(self)
  File "/usr/lib/python3.6/site-packages/celery/bootsteps.py", line 119, in start
    step.start(parent)
  File "/usr/lib/python3.6/site-packages/celery/bootsteps.py", line 369, in start
    return self.obj.start()
  File "/usr/lib/python3.6/site-packages/celery/worker/consumer/consumer.py", line 317, in start
    blueprint.start(self)
  File "/usr/lib/python3.6/site-packages/celery/bootsteps.py", line 119, in start
    step.start(parent)
  File "/usr/lib/python3.6/site-packages/celery/worker/consumer/consumer.py", line 593, in start
    c.loop(*c.loop_args())
  File "/usr/lib/python3.6/site-packages/celery/worker/loops.py", line 91, in asynloop
    next(loop)
  File "/usr/lib/python3.6/site-packages/kombu/asynchronous/hub.py", line 354, in create_loop
    cb(*cbargs)
  File "/usr/lib/python3.6/site-packages/kombu/transport/redis.py", line 1040, in on_readable
    self.cycle.on_readable(fileno)
  File "/usr/lib/python3.6/site-packages/kombu/transport/redis.py", line 337, in on_readable
    chan.handlers[type]()
  File "/usr/lib/python3.6/site-packages/kombu/transport/redis.py", line 667, in _receive
    ret.append(self._receive_one(c))
  File "/usr/lib/python3.6/site-packages/kombu/transport/redis.py", line 697, in _receive_one
    message, self._fanout_to_queue[exchange])
  File "/usr/lib/python3.6/site-packages/kombu/transport/virtual/base.py", line 983, in _deliver
    callback(message)
  File "/usr/lib/python3.6/site-packages/kombu/transport/virtual/base.py", line 633, in _callback
    return callback(message)
  File "/usr/lib/python3.6/site-packages/kombu/messaging.py", line 624, in _receive_callback
    return on_m(message) if on_m else self.receive(decoded, message)
  File "/usr/lib/python3.6/site-packages/celery/worker/consumer/gossip.py", line 201, in on_message
    _, event = prepare(message.payload)
  File "/usr/lib/python3.6/site-packages/kombu/message.py", line 207, in payload
    return self._decoded_cache if self._decoded_cache else self.decode()
  File "/usr/lib/python3.6/site-packages/kombu/message.py", line 192, in decode
    self._decoded_cache = self._decode()
  File "/usr/lib/python3.6/site-packages/kombu/message.py", line 197, in _decode
    self.content_encoding, accept=self.accept)
  File "/usr/lib/python3.6/site-packages/kombu/serialization.py", line 256, in loads
    raise self._for_untrusted_content(content_type, 'disabled')
kombu.exceptions.ContentDisallowed: Refusing to deserialize disabled content of type json (application/json)
```

I'd expect the workers to introduce themselves with a signed message. I can add `json` to the `content_types` config but that, again, totally defeats the purpose of signing these messages.

### No test coverage of the security features

I had a look at the coverage of these security features after having found these bugs. I was surprised by the fact that Codecov reports that these security modules don't have any test coverage. No actual code is tested: https://codecov.io/gh/celery/celery/tree/master/celery/security

So. Please tell me I have horribly misconfigured all of this. I'm not confident in the phrasing that "Celery is written with security in mind" (from the [docs](http://docs.celeryproject.org/en/latest/userguide/security.html)) if these are actual security bugs. I'm also worried about the millions of production systems, in which people may not even know that the security features may not even be turned on (also see "Security setup silently fails because of default settings").

Let me know if you need any more information. I'll try to actively participate in this discussion.
